title: Are Artificial Sweeteners Really Bad For You?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss artificial sweeteners and whether they are harmful. They cover the origins of diet soda, how sweetness is sensed, why many sweeteners are low or no calorie, accidental discoveries of saccharin and aspartame, FDA approval controversies (including the generally regarded as safe fast track), claims that diet soda drinkers gain weight (appetite and reward signaling), the saccharin bladder cancer rat studies, aspartame's breakdown into methanol and phenylketonuria, sucralose (Splenda), sugar alcohols and their laxative effect, and sweet-tasting proteins from rainforest plants. The episode opens with holiday banter and a Rat and Strip hair metal tangent, and closes with a listener mail segment from the Harvey family.

entities.name: Center for Science in the Public Interest

segments.title: Holiday return and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck welcome listeners back after the holidays, discuss dulcet tones, and Chuck's switch from soda to water. They introduce the topic of artificial sweeteners and the idea that they may be worse than sugar.

segments.title: Origins of diet soda and sweetness perception
segments.summary: The hosts explain that diet soda was originally marketed to people with diabetes and later to weight loss seekers. They describe how sweetness is sensed by receptors on the tongue and how sweeteners can be many times sweeter than sugar, making them low or no calorie.

segments.title: Accidental discoveries of sweeteners
segments.summary: Many artificial sweeteners were found by accident, including saccharin in 1879 by a chemist who did not wash his hands, and aspartame while researching an anti-ulcer drug. The hosts note that sugar is not the only sweet compound and that many sweet chemicals may remain undiscovered.

segments.title: Competition, cost, and the safety debate
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why there are many sweeteners, their different uses in baking and drinks, and cost advantages over sugar. They then describe the contested research on safety, anecdotal internet claims, and the industry-funded studies.

segments.title: FDA oversight and generally regarded as safe fast track
segments.summary: The hosts review the FDA's stated position that consumer complaints were investigated, and describe a fast track approval process in which companies submit literature reviews rather than their own data, which critics say leaves the FDA with little oversight.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Break between segments with off-topic banter about Brady Bunch and Cheers.

segments.title: Diet soda, appetite, and weight gain
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a Purdue study and the San Antonio Heart Study linking diet soda consumption with obesity. They explain the proposed mechanism: sweetness without satiety confuses the body's calorie signals and drives more eating and craving for sweet foods.

segments.title: Saccharin, Tab, and the bladder cancer rat studies
segments.summary: The hosts recount the saccharin bladder cancer findings in rats, which were tied to rat urine chemistry and not seen in humans, and the warning label on Tab that was removed in the late 1990s. Saccharin was removed from the NIH carcinogen list.

segments.title: Aspartame breakdown, methanol, and PKU
segments.summary: The hosts explain that aspartame breaks down into phenylalanine and methanol, the risk for people with phenylketonuria, and EPA methanol limits compared with the amount in a liter of aspartame-sweetened drink. They mention a rat study linking aspartame to cancers in female rats.

segments.title: Sucralose, Splenda, and stevia
segments.summary: The hosts describe sucralose as chlorinated sugar marketed as made from sugar, the sugar industry lawsuit, a mouse cell genetic damage finding, and its heat stability in baked goods. They also contrast Stevia, which comes from a plant, with Sweet'N Low and Splenda.

segments.title: Sugar alcohols and sweet-tasting proteins
segments.summary: The hosts describe sugar alcohols used in sugar free gum and their laxative effects, with differing FDA and CSPI positions on labeling. They close by discussing sweet-tasting proteins from rainforest plants as a possible alternative.

segments.title: Listener mail from the Harvey family
segments.summary: A listener named Grace writes that she and her sisters have listened to the podcast on road trips with their dad since 2009, and mention favorite episodes.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck give social media and contact information and sign off.
